contributions.item_title_en: 7. Reform UK Debate: Wales and the United Kingdom
contributions.text_english:
Addressing the motion before us, let me remind Members what the First Minister promised before the election. It was to establish a national commission on Wales's constitutional feature, not push for independence after 100 days. Yet after meeting the leaders of Sinn Féin and the SNP, this administration now appears to be charging full pelt towards independence. The joint Plaid, Sinn Féin and SNP agreement declares, and I quote,

‘Momentum is behind our movements; we believe that constitutional change is coming.’

The people of Wales deserve to know exactly what that means, exactly what it will cost, and exactly who will pay. Only last year, the First Minister declared that there was business to do right now. That meant, he stated, improvements in health, education, families, jobs, the environment and farming. And on that point, I agree. There is business to do, urgent business, serious business, and yet, instead of getting on with that, we seem to be heading down a constitutional rabbit hole.

Welsh families are worried about the Welsh NHS. They're worried about the cost of living. They're worried about whether their children will find jobs and build a future. And what is the answer from Plaid Cymru? More division, more distraction, more constitutional theatre.

After 100 days, this administration should be focused on what matters to the people of Wales. Patients are still waiting too long for treatment. Front-line services remain under pressure, and unemployment is too high. Energy bills for households and business are disastrous. Breaking the union will not fix any of this; it will make it worse.

And then there is the cost. Wales simply cannot afford the independence experiment. The Office for National Statistics demonstrated that the net fiscal deficit for Wales in 2024-25 was between £22 billion and £23 billion. And your own Minister, Dafydd Trystan Davies, Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution stated, and I quote,

‘it is plainly evident that Wales is a net fiscal beneficiary of the United Kingdom.’

What would be needed to pay for this? The answer: higher taxes and more borrowing. This is not a plan. It is a slow-motion fiscal car crash dressed up as a national project. And who pays? Who picks up the bill? The answer is simple: the Welsh taxpayer, Welsh families.

Leaving the United Kingdom would mean walking away from the benefits of a larger union, shared resources, fiscal transfers and economic scale. It's a gamble with people's jobs, mortgages, pensions—a gamble doomed to failure.

Then there is the plan to devolve the Crown Estate. This isn't the magic bullet Plaid claim. There is no Scottish-style windfall and no pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. The Welsh Government's own expert group said gross revenues would probably be less than £20 million a year—£20 million—and that is before the cost of creating another Welsh quango. It is obvious that all that Wales gains from being part of the United Kingdom is strength, financial security and shared opportunity. [Interruption.] No, sorry, can I just finish?

Being part of the union does not weaken Wales; it makes us stronger. The Senedd already has extensive powers over health, transport and education, so before Plaid Cymru put all their energy into breaking the union, they should answer a straightforward question: what have they done so far with the powers they already possess? What do the people of Wales actually want? Poll after poll after poll, the majority do not support independence. They want the Government to stop talking to itself and start listening to them. Welsh people want action that will revive the Welsh industry. Businesses, again, and energy-intensive industries in Wales are being squeezed by massive energy costs and bureaucracy—costs that prevent further investment, make them uncompetitive, and jobs are being lost. We need an energy policy built on affordability, reliability and national security. We need to scrap 'net stupid zero'. We should reassess the energy mix and support the roll-out of small modular nuclear reactors.

Wales's industry needs dependable power to be able to grow. The task will be impossible if we aren't part of the United Kingdom. The Welsh people want NHS waiting lists fixed. We need to clear the backlogs for all NHS treatments. The NHS needs more doctors, nurses and fewer managers. Welsh farming needs more support, not regulation. In Wales, we need farmers to produce more food. We should let farmers produce food, protect the countryside and sustain rural communities. Reform choose the United Kingdom. We need real action over pipe dreams and we need to keep Wales strong within the United Kingdom. Diolch.

contributions.text_english: 7. What action is the Welsh Government taking to reduce river pollution levels in Carmarthenshire? OQ64555
contributions.text_original: 7. Pa gamau y mae Llywodraeth Cymru yn eu cymryd i leihau lefelau llygredd afonydd yn Sir Gaerfyrddin? OQ64555

contributions.text_english:
Diolch, First Minister. People whose livelihoods depend on Carmarthenshire's rivers, including members of Carmarthen Coracle and Netsmen's Association, tell us they have never seen such a poor season, with the return of only six sewin from May to June this year. Their experience makes clear that river pollution must be treated with a far greater urgency. I urge you to read the Royal Society's recent report on chemical mixtures in British waterways. Quote: 'Regulators are flying blind.' Unquote.

In Carmarthenshire, Natural Resources Wales seem to be flying blind. Our rivers are being contaminated by harmful chemical mixtures, including organics, ammonia, microplastics, cadmium and mercury, with no understanding of their interactions or the harm done. Will you acknowledge that the Welsh Government lacks a credible plan to clean up our rivers, and set out how it will meet its political duty to protect our waters and rivers and special areas of conservation?

contributions.text_english: 4. Will the First Minister make a statement on waiting times for cataract surgery in Sir Gaerfyrddin? OQ64456
contributions.text_original: 4. A wnaiff y Prif Weinidog ddatganiad ar amseroedd aros am lawdriniaeth cataractau yn Sir Gaerfyrddin? OQ64456

contributions.text_english: Diolch, First Minister. Despite your Government's investment, including the use of higher cost private providers, and the appointment of a Deputy Minister for Public and Preventative Health, my constituents still face long waits and last-minute cancellations of cataract operations. What long-term action will the Welsh Government take to train more eye surgeons and increase capacity to meet the growing demand from an ageing population, including patients with glaucoma or diabetic retinopathy and those needing regular eye injections to prevent avoidable blindness?

contributions.text_english: Diolch, Deputy Presiding Officer. Trefnydd, I would like to call for a Welsh Government statement on what support can be provided to constituents and local communities who wish to challenge the actions of well-funded infrastructure developers. As you will know, High Court proceedings are simply beyond the means of most families. Many of the constituents that I represent in Carmarthenshire have been subjected to survey notices that the High Court found were not issued in accordance with the statutory scheme. Concerned landowners and occupiers have faced significant stress and expenses because of the actions that they have been subjected to. They would welcome reassurances from this Welsh Government on what support can be provided to them. Therefore, I call for a Welsh Government statement on this matter. Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
contributions.text_english: People across Carmarthenshire are no longer confused by the language around net zero, they are frustrated by it, because when Ministers talk about strategic investment and a just transition, many hear spin. What they actually see are higher bills, disruption in their communities and decisions being imposed upon them. We were told this would protect the environment, but tell that to the residents in the Tywi valley facing proposed pylons and 200-metre wind turbines dominating their landscape. Tell that to the people in Bynea and Pumsaint dealing with vast solar developments—years of dust, noise and disruption. And we were promised lower bills, yet families are seeing that the opposite is happening. So, will the Minister answer this directly: where is the evidence this approach is delivering for ordinary people? And will the Government change course if this continues to drive up costs and lose public consent? Diolch.

contributions.item_title_en: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability: Priorities for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
contributions.text_english:
Minister, what I hear across Carmarthenshire is simple: people do not feel more resilient—they feel under pressure. Farmers are being asked to do more, comply with more, and absorb more cost—from TB to the SFS to the rise in diesel costs and fertiliser costs. Margins are being squeezed tighter than ever. And at the same time, we are not securing the future. Where is the clear plan to bring through the next generation of farmers who will actually feed us into the future?

And it's not just farming. Rural businesses, pubs, B&Bs and tourism operators are struggling to stay afloat, yet they are confronted with a tourism tax, a 182-day rule. They see it as punishing, not supporting. Their survival is on the brink. So let's be frank—these policies may well be well intentioned, but on the ground they are being felt as burdens, not support. Minister, if this agenda is about resilience and sustainability, why do so many in rural Wales feel less resilient and less sustainable? Diolch.

contributions.text_english: Across Carmarthenshire, from Pumsaint to Bynea, from Ferryside to the Tywi valley, people are angry, First Minister. They see their countryside being industrialised with massive wind turbines, huge solar sites, substations, and miles and miles of pylons. There's concrete, disruption and destruction on their productive farmland. What angers them most, First Minister, is that, during the campaign, Plaid Cymru stood with these communities, nodding along to their concerns, offering warm words and so-called alternatives, but now they're in Government, those same communities feel completely abandoned. So let me ask you directly: was this just lip service to get elected? Are rural communities in Carmarthenshire now simply being told they must sacrifice their land, their farming, their tourism, their way of life to satisfy your ideological obsession with net zero, no matter what the cost? Why would anyone trust Plaid Cymru again when it says one thing on the doorstep and does the exact opposite in Government? Diolch.
